title: Clean Code and Maintainability
learning_outcomes: Explain the central rule or purpose of clean code and maintainability using at least one correct term from the lesson.
Interpret or adapt a small Kotlin example that demonstrates clean code and maintainability.
Identify one relevant edge case, debugging step, or version/platform constraint.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn **Clean Code and Maintainability** as part of **Software Engineering, Security, and Performance**. Readable names, focused functions, explicit ownership, and low-coupling module boundaries reduce maintenance cost. Use the subtopics—Small, Focused Functions, Naming and Readability, Avoiding Overengineering—as a checklist: predict what the example will do, then verify it in a project configured for the target platform.
content.why_it_matters: Professional applications need repeatable tests, clear APIs, dependable dependencies, security checks, and observable failures. Apply this concept in small steps before integrating it into a larger project.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Readable names, focused functions, explicit ownership, and low-coupling module boundaries reduce maintenance cost.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with small, focused functions. Then compare it with naming and readability. Identify the input, state, dependency, or branch that determines the result. The snippet is a static reference for CodeLeaf and is not executed in the lesson page.

items.title: Small, Focused Functions
items.text: Small, Focused Functions describes how behavior is declared, passed, or composed. Make inputs and return types clear, keep side effects visible, and use a small call-site example to judge readability.

items.title: Naming and Readability
items.text: Naming and Readability is one part of clean code and maintainability. Connect its definition to the example, identify the input/state it changes, and verify the expected behavior with a small test case.

items.title: Avoiding Overengineering
items.text: Avoiding Overengineering is one part of clean code and maintainability. Connect its definition to the example, identify the input/state it changes, and verify the expected behavior with a small test case.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in the project that declares the necessary JVM, coroutine, networking, database, or serialization dependencies. Never commit real secrets.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the documented starting values, rerun the smallest test, and compare the result with the expected output. If behavior differs, check the compiler/plugin/runtime versions and the active target before changing more than one thing.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Clean Code and Maintainability removes the need to test boundary conditions or verify the chosen runtime/library version.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the example fails, first confirm which runtime/project type the snippet requires. Read the first useful compiler or runtime message, check imports and declared dependencies, reduce the example to a minimal case, and rerun. For target-specific code, use the target toolchain rather than assuming a console or browser runner can execute it.

items.title: Explain
items.text: Describe the main rule of clean code and maintainability in your own words.

items.title: Apply
items.text: Change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

items.title: Verify
items.text: Check one edge case and the official reference for the selected Kotlin/runtime version.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small variation that demonstrates clean code and maintainability. Write down your predicted result first, run it in the correct local project, then explain one boundary case involving small, focused functions.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain clean code and maintainability without copying the lesson wording.
Demonstrate the concept with a small code/configuration change and state the expected result.
Test one boundary case or explain a relevant platform/version limitation.
hints: Begin with the first syllabus subtopic: Small, Focused Functions. What input or state does it act on?
Change only one value, branch, declaration, or dependency at a time. Predict what should happen before running the code.
Compare your observed result with the expected output and the official reference; verify that you are using the required project type and dependency set.
